The contents include acknowledgments, abbreviations, an executive summary, rationale for the guidelines, objectives, methods, recommendations, and an overview of the guidelines for the prevention, treatment, and management of sexually transmitted infections (STIs). It also includes specific sections on the epidemiology and burden of STIs, the need for updated guidelines, and the approach to revising STI guidelines. The WHO guidelines for the treatment of genital herpes simplex virus (HSV) provide evidence-based recommendations for managing this condition. Genital HSV is a significant public health concern due to its high prevalence and its role in facilitating the transmission of human immunodeficiency virus (HIV). HSV type 2 (HSV-2) is the most common cause of genital ulcers globally, with an estimated 417 million people infected in 2012. HSV type 1 (HSV-1), traditionally associated with oral infections, is increasingly recognized as a cause of genital herpes, particularly in high-income countries. HSV-2 infection is of particular concern due to its epidemiological synergy with HIV. Individuals with HSV-2 are approximately three times more likely to acquire HIV, and those co-infected with HIV and genital HSV are more likely to transmit HIV to others. Genital HSV is a lifelong condition characterized by frequent symptomatic recurrences, although most initial infections are asymptomatic or atypical. Laboratory testing is often required to differentiate between HSV-1 and HSV-2 infections and to rule out other causes of genital ulcers. The guidelines recommend antiviral treatment for the first clinical episode of genital HSV infection, with acyclovir being the preferred medication due to its lower cost compared to valacyclovir and famciclovir. Dosage regimens for acyclovir include 400 mg orally three times daily for 10 days or 200 mg orally five times daily for 10 days. For recurrent episodes, episodic therapy should be initiated within 24 hours of symptom onset, and suppressive therapy is suggested for individuals with frequent, severe, or distressing recurrences. Suppressive therapy should be reassessed after one year. The burden of STIs, including HSV, is significant worldwide, with over one million curable STIs acquired daily. In 2012, there were an estimated 357 million new cases of curable STIs among adults aged 15–49 years, including chlamydia, gonorrhea, syphilis, and trichomoniasis. Viral STIs, such as HSV-2 and human papillomavirus (HPV), are also highly prevalent. Untreated STIs can lead to severe complications, including infertility, ectopic pregnancy, miscarriage, and congenital infections. Maternal syphilis alone resulted in 350,000 adverse pregnancy outcomes in 2012. The prevention and control of STIs are integral to achieving universal health coverage and related Sustainable Development Goals. Updated global guidelines are essential to address changes in STI epidemiology, antimicrobial resistance patterns, and advancements in prevention, diagnosis, and treatment. For example, resistance to previously recommended treatments for gonorrhea and other STIs necessitates the development of new treatment protocols. The guidelines also emphasize the importance of incorporating rapid diagnostic tests into syndromic management and expanding access to vaccines for HPV and HSV-2. Countries are strongly encouraged to adapt these updated global guidelines to their local epidemiological and antimicrobial resistance data.
